metadata.title: How context shapes the relationship between school autonomy and test-scores. An explanatory analysis using PISA 2015

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses student-level data from PISA 2015 and focuses on 34 countries with sufficient within-country variation in school autonomy. The dependent variable is PISA math performance, and observations are weighted according to each student’s probability of selection to reflect the population of 15-year-old students in each country. For variance estimation, the authors use Balanced Repeated Replication (BRR) with Fay’s adjustment, consistent with PISA replication procedures. The paper also uses the first plausible value for math as the main specification, and reports robustness to excluding weights and to using other plausible values, indicating that the core conclusions are not driven solely by the weighting/PV choices.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses PISA 2015 student-level data and restricts to 34 countries with sufficient within-country variation in school autonomy. Countries are excluded if autonomy information is representative only for parts of the country, if autonomy data are missing, or if there is not enough within-country variation in autonomy. To ensure variation, included countries must have at least 20% but no more than 95% of schools with hiring autonomy. The analytic sample further excludes student and school observations with missing values for any critical variables in the models, resulting in loss of up to 18% of schools and up to 22% of student observations across the included countries.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Math (first plausible value), pooled across 34 countries
main_findings.target_variable: PISA math achievement (Plausible Values; first PV)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pooled OLS (weighted by selection probability; BRR with Fay adjustment). R2 ranges from 0.03 (bivariate) to 0.41 (with controls and country fixed effects). Key coefficients (with country fixed effects + controls): Budget autonomy = +4.62 points (significant, p<0.05); other autonomy types become null.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Math the study leveraged hiring, budget, course-content, and admissions autonomy (plus student and school controls) to analyze PISA math achievement, finding that autonomy coefficients are highly sensitive to specification and largely become null once selection-related controls and country fixed effects are included, with only budget autonomy showing a small positive association. This indicates that apparent autonomy–achievement relationships in simple models are likely driven by selective implementation and context, so policy evaluations should control for student/school sorting and country context rather than relying on unconditional correlations.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Math (first plausible value), pooled across 34 countries
main_findings.target_variable: Gender achievement gap (boys vs girls) at non-autonomous vs autonomous schools
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pooled OLS with country fixed effects; BRR with Fay adjustment; clustered SE at school level. Subgroup gaps at non-autonomous schools are significant: Female subgroup coefficients range from -9 to -19 points (p<0.05). Autonomy interaction effects (subgroup x autonomy) are ambiguous overall; significant β3 patterns include budget and content autonomy decreasing gender gaps (negative β3) in some specifications/countries.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Math the study leveraged autonomy types and female subgroup membership to estimate gender achievement gaps at non-autonomous versus autonomous schools, finding that gender gaps are present in non-autonomous schools but autonomy-related changes to gaps are inconsistent across autonomy forms and countries, with some evidence that budget and content autonomy can reduce gender gaps while other autonomy forms show null or opposite patterns. This indicates that decentralization may affect equity differently by policy design and context, so autonomy reforms should be paired with equity-focused monitoring rather than assuming uniform gap reduction.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Math (first plausible value), pooled across 34 countries
main_findings.target_variable: Wealth achievement gap (top 4 quintiles vs bottom quintile) at non-autonomous vs autonomous schools
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pooled OLS with country fixed effects; BRR with Fay adjustment; clustered SE at school level. Subgroup gaps at non-autonomous schools are significant: Bottom wealth quintile coefficients range from -6 to -17 points (p<0.05). Autonomy interaction effects are mostly not consistently significant in pooled models, but country-level patterns show that autonomy can either reduce or increase wealth gaps depending on autonomy type and context.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Math the study leveraged autonomy types and bottom-wealth subgroup membership to estimate wealth gaps at non-autonomous versus autonomous schools, finding that wealth gaps are robust in non-autonomous schools while autonomy-related changes to gaps are heterogeneous across countries and autonomy forms. This indicates that autonomy reforms can either mitigate or exacerbate socioeconomic inequities depending on how autonomy is implemented, so policymakers should evaluate equity outcomes at the country and subgroup level rather than using pooled averages.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Math (first plausible value), pooled across 34 countries
main_findings.target_variable: Parent education achievement gap (mother with college degree vs without) at non-autonomous vs autonomous schools
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pooled OLS with country fixed effects; BRR with Fay adjustment; clustered SE at school level. Subgroup gaps at non-autonomous schools are significant: Mother-without-college coefficients range from -10 to -19 points (p<0.05). Autonomy interaction effects (subgroup x autonomy) are ambiguous in pooled models; significant patterns include content autonomy increasing parent-education gaps in some specifications/countries.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Math the study leveraged autonomy types and mother-education subgroup membership to estimate parent-education gaps at non-autonomous versus autonomous schools, finding that parent-education gaps are substantial in non-autonomous schools but autonomy can either reduce or increase these gaps depending on autonomy type and country context. This indicates that decentralization may shift resources or incentives in ways that do not uniformly protect disadvantaged students, so equity safeguards and accountability design should be considered alongside autonomy.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Math (first plausible value), restricted to autonomous schools
main_findings.target_variable: Achievement gaps under autonomy with vs without test-based accountability
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pooled OLS with country fixed effects; BRR with Fay adjustment; clustered SE at school level; sample restricted to schools reporting autonomy. In pooled models, accountability interaction terms are mostly small and not statistically significant, while subgroup gaps remain significant (gender gaps ~6–9 points; wealth gaps ~16–19 points; parent-education gaps ~15–18 points). Country-level disaggregation shows cases where gaps exist only with accountability or only without accountability.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Math data restricted to autonomous schools, the study leveraged test-based accountability (public achievement reporting) and subgroup membership to estimate whether accountability changes achievement gaps, finding that pooled interaction effects are generally not significant while country-level results show inconsistent patterns (gaps sometimes appear only with or only without accountability). This indicates that coupling autonomy with accountability does not guarantee equity improvements, so policymakers should design accountability systems carefully and assess their effects empirically by context.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2015 student-level data (math achievement) pooled across 34 countries selected for sufficient within-country variation in school autonomy. The dependent variable is the first plausible value for PISA math, and models are estimated with pooled OLS including country fixed effects, student controls (gender, age, nativity, mother’s education, wealth) and school controls (rural location, public funding, enrollment, and composition by wealth and mother’s education). The key results show that autonomy–achievement associations are highly sensitive to specification: unconditional models suggest sizable effects, but once selection-related controls and country fixed effects are added, most autonomy coefficients become null, with only budget autonomy showing a small positive association (~+4.62 points). For equity, gender, wealth, and parent-education gaps are substantial in non-autonomous schools, while autonomy and accountability effects on gaps are heterogeneous across countries. The paper is not an ML prediction study (no ML algorithms are trained), and causal interpretation is limited because the design explicitly focuses on associations and selection bias rather than causal identification.
